sub_questions: Which FPGA/Verilog projects are easy enough for a 4th-year B.Tech ECE team (one or two semesters, low-cost board) yet offer genuine novelty?

What makes an FPGA project publishable — what contribution (comparison, optimization, new application, resource/power/latency improvement) do IEEE conferences and Scopus journals accept for such work?
Which specific project ideas rank best on the novelty vs ease vs publishability trade-off, with tools, board, and expected results?

How should students write and structure the research paper (IEEE format, results tables: LUTs/FFs/DSPs, Fmax, power, latency; comparison with prior work) and where to submit (IEEE conferences, Scopus-indexed journals) while avoiding predatory venues?
required_formats: ranked comparison table of project ideas (novelty / ease / publishability)
required_section_headings: ## 1. What Makes an FPGA Project Both Easy and Publishable
## 3. Recommended Project: Scope, Tools, and Novelty Angle
## 5. Where to Publish: IEEE Conferences and Scopus Journals
scope_conditions: FPGA with Verilog HDL coding (not VHDL-only, not ASIC-only)
must be the easiest feasible while still novel
paper targeted at IEEE conference or Scopus-indexed journal

levers.domain_notes: Sourcing: IEEE Xplore/arXiv/open-access papers showing published undergraduate-scale FPGA work with resource/power/timing tables; vendor docs (AMD Xilinx Vivado, Intel Quartus, open-source Yosys); publication-ethics sources (IEEE author center, Scopus source list, UGC-CARE/predatory-journal guidance). Evidence norms: prefer published FPGA papers with measurable LUT/Fmax/power/latency results and comparisons. Recency: last 3 years for novelty angles.

rationale.register: user asks to be told the best easy+novel project to do, i.e. a recommendation
rationale.inference_depth: needs linking project ideas to publication evidence
